places.name: Lễ Tuyền Phái
places.size: A minor sect of healers and brewers, now only the old Spring House since the sect moved to Triêu Hà Hồ in 1141: about 70 people in its day (25 healers, 45 cellar hands), a walled compound about 400 m across with about 40 buildings.
places.where: Grassland at 20 m, inland, a low rise by the lake shore of the rice plain. Earth qi. A vassal of Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the hot spring Cam Lộ Thang 75 km, the lake Bạc Hà Đàm 125 km. Map crop: a low golden-green rise just east of a long blue lake about 80 km wide that runs off the frame north and south, with a ridge of bare grey crags and the sea beyond its far shore; a river runs south from the lake to a small bay.
places.imagined: Late morning. A white stone basin brimming under an enormous wutong, rows of red-clay-sealed jars warming in the sun.
places.subject: The place: Lễ Tuyền Phái, the Spring House of a sect of healers, seen from above open grassland. Setting: a low rise on a wide green and golden plain above the east shore of a huge still lake that runs off the frame north and south, a ridge of bare grey crags and the sea beyond its far shore, and rice plain and thin lines of poplar stretching away east. The compound is about four hundred metres across, within a low whitewashed wall, on three shallow terraces: about forty pale timber buildings, a short stack of three halls, a three-roofed pagoda, dormitories, herb-drying sheds, and long low cellars with turf roofs. Below the pagoda lies a round basin of white stone, about twenty metres across, brimming with clear spring water under one enormous wutong tree whose broad leaves glisten wet; a channel leads water away to the herb gardens. On the lowest terrace stand rows of stoneware jars, perhaps three hundred, sealed with red clay, warming in the sun, with brewers tending them. Gourd ladles hang on pegs beside the basin, no metal. Around the walls are neat herb gardens in square beds and a small orchard, a rice field, and a road of beaten earth. Perhaps thirty figures in cream robes: porters with jars, gardeners, a healer treating a sick man on a cart. Golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Eleven cellar tunnels, roofed with turf, run back under the rise, and the stoneware jars are carried down them on two-wheeled barrows. A gourd-ladle shed stands beside the basin with forty ladles hung on pegs. The three-roofed pagoda has a green tile roof, and a gong tower beside it is struck at dusk. Along the south wall is a row of copper stills with bamboo pipes, and a line of eight white cloths hangs over the herb beds to dry. The healers' ward, a long low house with open sides, has rows of cots, each with a gourd cup.

places.name: Lai Nghi Thành
places.size: A walled port city: wall about 2.5 km across, some 15,000 roofs and about 70,000 people, with a harbour mole about 1 km long carrying a nine-tiered terrace, protected by a guardian array.
places.where: Dry steppe at sea level at a river mouth on the east coast of the gulf. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung, founded 530. The old book: when the Shao music was played nine times the phoenix came. Nearest: the spirit vein Cửu Tấu Mạch 75 km, the ruin Vân Môn Thành 141 km. Map crop: a river mouth on the north shore of a blue bay, with rolling golden-green hills inland and a bank of bare grey crags at the upper left; a lake or river valley runs north from the city.
places.imagined: Sunrise. Nine stepped tiers glinting with bronze bell frames, musicians climbing one tier at a time.
places.subject: The place: Lai Nghi Thành, the City where the Phoenix Comes, seen from above the gulf at sunrise. Setting: a dry pale-gold steppe rolling inland in low hills, a bank of bare grey crags faint at the upper left, a river mouth with sandbars opening into a calm blue gulf, a low shore. The city is a walled port about two and a half kilometres across, grey-brown brick walls with twelve gate towers and a faint shimmer in the air over them that marks its guardian array, a dome of pale light like a bubble. Inside are about fifteen thousand grey and ochre tile roofs, laid in ward blocks around a broad avenue from the northern gate to the harbour, a large central square, canals from the river, drying-yards and salt warehouses, and two big temples with yellow roofs. A harbour mole curves a kilometre out into the gulf, forming a sheltered basin with forty ships and fishing boats. On the mole rises a terrace of nine stepped stone tiers, each about twenty metres broader than the one above, each crowned with a bronze bell frame, so that the whole stair glints gold at sunrise; musicians in red robes climb the tiers in a line, tiny figures. Rice barges and desert caravans of camels both arrive at the quays. Low golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Inside the walls the avenue to the mole is wide enough for forty marching musicians abreast. Nine round stone drums, each three metres wide, stand along its length, one for each tier, and a long covered colonnade runs beside the harbour. The bronze bell frames carry about a hundred and forty bells in all. Salt boats and rice barges unload on the river side, and caravans of camels wait outside the north gate in a long picket line. The guardian array's shimmer stands highest over the central drum tower.

places.name: Hoàng Vân Thành
places.size: A granary city: wall about 3 km across, some 20,000 roofs and about 90,000 people, with a ring of about thirty round granaries at its heart.
places.where: Grassland at 50 m on a river where the rice plain lies flattest. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the beast lair Dã Trư Lâm 75 km, the village Ngân Hạnh 150 km. Fed the south in the drought of 649. Map crop: a broad river running through a gold-green plain, with bare grey mountains and dark forest on the west and the sea showing beyond them; a pond lies south-west of the city.
places.imagined: Harvest. A golden haze of rice chaff over the roofs at low sun, grain barges crowding the quay.
places.subject: The place: Hoàng Vân Thành, Yellow Cloud City, seen from above the flattest part of a great rice plain at harvest. Setting: a vast plain of rice paddies in gold and green squares reaching to the east horizon with a grey rocky ridge and dark forest to the west and the sea glimpsed beyond them, with a broad brown river cutting across, and rows of poplar. The city is a broad walled square about three kilometres across, with thick earthen-brick walls, twelve gate towers and a deep moat, enclosing about twenty thousand roofs of grey tile in regular ward blocks and canals. At the centre, inside an inner wall, stands a ring of about thirty tall round granaries, each thirty metres across, capped with yellow-glazed conical tile roofs, around a central yard, with two even larger granaries in the middle. Over all the roofs hangs a haze of rice chaff, turned gold in the low sun, which gives the city its name. Outside the walls a river quay about a kilometre long is crowded by hundreds of grain barges, with long queues of ox-carts piled with sacks entering the granary gates and porters in lines. Threshing floors and winnowing sheds line the roads. Fine golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right, and a sense of enormous plenty. Each of the thirty granaries holds about forty thousand sacks, and a keeper's house stands against every one with a lamp that burns all night. A ring road two hundred metres wide separates the granaries from the first houses, kept clear for fire-carts. Chaff drifts in a golden cloud that is thickest above the quay. On the river there are two floating weighing-houses, and the barge queue stretches for three kilometres downstream, each barge flying nothing but a plain brown awning.

places.name: Đạo Hương Trấn
places.size: A small walled rice town of about 1,000 roofs and 4,500 people, wall about 700 m across, plus a long row of stone stakes along the east road.
places.where: Grassland at 10 m on a river in the rice plain. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the lake Minh Kính Hồ 79 km, the village Ngân Hạnh 152 km. The Vương family settled in 520. Map crop: a slow river running through green-gold plain to a long blue lake lying just south of the town, with a bare grey ridge and the sea beyond to the west.
places.imagined: Ripening rice. A long row of carved stone stakes, one for each generation, each beside its paddy.
places.subject: The place: Đạo Hương Trấn, Rice Scent Town, seen from above a sea of ripening rice. Setting: a flat green-gold plain of paddies in every shape, divided by dykes and channels that shine with water, a slow river curving by to a long blue lake just south of the town, a bare grey ridge and the sea beyond it to the west, and low hills far behind. The town is small and walled, about seven hundred metres across, a grey brick wall with four gates and a square tower, enclosing about a thousand grey-tile roofs in tight lanes, a market yard, a granary with a thatched roof, a temple, and a mill by the river. A single road runs out of the east gate across the fields. Along it stands a long row of carved stone stakes, about twenty, each waist-high, each set beside one particular paddy of different shape and age, so that the row reads as a procession of generations: the nearest paddies are old and irregular, the last ones new and square, and the stakes are spaced widely. Farmers in broad hats wade in the nearest paddies, a water buffalo drags a harrow, children sit on the stakes, and an old woman walks the road with a basket. Heavy ripening scent seems to hang in the air, with a faint haze. Warm light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The stakes are of grey stone, each carved on top with a small stylised paddy and on its face with the planter's name and the year; the oldest are weathered nearly smooth. Between the town and the lake lie the oldest fields, narrow terraces of black mud. In the market square sits a matchmakers' arcade of twelve tables, each with a ledger, and a small group of them, tiny figures in plum-coloured robes, gather around a letterbox whose lid stands open. Water buffalo wallow beside the east gate.

places.name: Lục Dã Trấn
places.size: A walled herb town of about 1,200 roofs and 5,500 people, wall about 800 m across, ringed by about 200 square herb beds.
places.where: Grassland at 10 m, inland. Earth qi. Held by Lễ Tuyền Phái. Nearest: the lake Bạc Hà Đàm 75 km, the lake Triêu Hà Hồ 90 km. Map crop: a gentle green meadow on the east shore of a long blue lake that touches the town's west side, with a bare grey ridge beyond the lake and the sea farther west.
places.imagined: Early morning, herb beds steaming, a smell of mint and bitter root.
places.subject: The place: Lục Dã Trấn, Green Meadow Town, seen from above open green meadows. Setting: gentle meadows and low hills with a long blue lake lying against the town's western side, a bare grey ridge beyond it and the sea farther west, and morning mist. The town is walled, about eight hundred metres across, a grey stone wall with four gate towers and a spring-fed moat, enclosing about twelve hundred grey-tile roofs, a cross of two main streets, a small healers' hall with a green roof, a well-house, and drying yards. Around the town spreads a chequer of about two hundred square herb beds in a dozen shades of green, from pale mint to dark bitter-root, silver-grey sage to blue-green, each bordered by a low stone channel of spring water, so the whole meadow looks like a patchwork quilt of green squares crossed by silver lines. In the morning the beds steam faintly. At the town gate stands a small stone spring channel with a basin, and a woman holds a newborn over it. Dozens of gardeners in pale robes kneel in the beds, cutters carry baskets of fresh leaves to drying sheds with slatted walls, small carts of herbs in bundles queue at the gate. Light from the upper left, mist, soft long shadows. Each bed is about thirty metres square, and the channels are fed from a single main spring-pipe that runs under the town in a stone culvert and fans out into branches. At the east gate stands the drying hall, a long shed with open slatted sides and rows of racks hung with bunches of herb. A healers' lodge with a green roof sits near the gate, and a small mint-green banner-less pole stands in front. The street along the lakeshore is lined with willows, and washerwomen kneel on stone steps beating cloth in the lake.

places.name: Thủy Điền Thôn
places.size: A village of about 30 houses and 130 people on a low dyke among the oldest rice paddies on the plain, with one great waterwheel.
places.where: Grassland at 60 m, inland on a river. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the spirit vein Hòa Miêu Mạch 79 km, the city Hoàng Vân 152 km. Rice first planted here in 140. Map crop: a river running through a gold-green plain, bare grey mountains to the west and orange-brown hills to the north-west; a small pond at the east edge.
places.imagined: Spring, flooded fields, a great bamboo waterwheel creaking round.
places.subject: The place: Thủy Điền Thôn, Flooded Field Village, seen from above in early spring. Setting: a flat plain of flooded paddies, glassy mirrors of sky and cloud divided by dykes in an irregular pattern, the oldest on the plain, with a slow river along one edge, bare grey mountains on the horizon to the west and orange-brown hills to the north-west. The village sits on a low dyke, about thirty grey-tile houses in two short rows with yards, a drying floor, a well, a small shrine, and a few buffalo sheds. On the riverbank stands a great bamboo waterwheel twelve metres across, its rim strung with tube buckets, lifting water into a wooden trough that feeds a branching network of irrigation channels leading into the fields. Farmers bend in the flooded fields in long rows planting seedlings, some forty tiny figures in conical hats, while a child at the very front sets the first seedling at the head of the oldest field, with the others waiting. Green seedling lines fan out in perfect curves. Egrets stand in the paddies. Footpaths along the dykes are lined with water. Pale spring light from the upper left, long soft shadows. The paddy walls are of beaten earth, each topped with a line of grass, and the plan of the fields is an irregular patchwork, the first fields at the village's feet, new fields spreading outward in neater squares. The waterwheel's trough runs along the dyke for sixty metres before branching. In front of the oldest field stands a small stone with a worn seedling carved on it. Three buffalo plough in a line, and a plank-and-rope bridge crosses the river at the south end of the dyke.

places.name: Âu Lộ Thôn
places.size: A village of about 25 houses and 110 people at the landward edge of a marsh, beside a dead-tree rookery about 2 km across.
places.where: Low marsh grassland at sea level on the east coast of the gulf. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the spirit vein Thanh Âu Nhãn 100 km. Pearl divers from the burned harbour settled here in 763. Map crop: a forested headland pushing north into a wide blue gulf, with open sea on three sides, golden-green hills behind it; the marsh is only a small cove at the headland's tip.
places.imagined: Dawn. A stand of dead white trees loud with gulls and herons, houses set back with empty diving baskets hung over the doors.
places.subject: The place: Âu Lộ Thôn, Gull and Heron Village, seen from above a low marsh shore. Setting: a dark forested headland pushing north into a wide blue gulf, with a small cove of reed marsh, mud flats and sandbars at its tip and open sea on three sides. A stand of dead trees about two kilometres across stands in the water, leafless grey trunks bleached white by droppings and nesting gulls and herons, thousands of them, so the whole stand looks snowed on, and clouds of birds wheel above in the dawn light. At the landward edge of the marsh, well back from the waterline, stand about twenty-five low houses of grey stone and thatch, in a loose line with small yards, drying racks for fish, nets, and a few small boats pulled up in a channel. On the walls of the houses hang old diving baskets and weighted ropes, dry, and above every door an empty basket. Villagers fish from the shore with long poles and cast nets, tiny figures; nobody puts to sea. Pale dawn light from the upper left, pink-grey sky, mist on the water. The rookery's trees stand in water up to their knees, and the guano-white drifts have reached the first houses' yards. Diving baskets of woven reed, the size of a barrel, hang in rows along each house front, empty, dozens in all, with weighted ropes coiled beside them. A plank road crosses the marsh to a landing with two small punts, and there is a fish-smoking shed at its end. Beyond the village forest paths lead up the headland to a lookout hut.

places.name: Ngân Hạnh Thôn
places.size: A village of about 40 houses and 180 people under one colossal ginkgo about 60 m tall with a crown 90 m across.
places.where: Temperate forest at 40 m on a small river among oak woods at the edge of the plain. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the ruin Ngọc Quản Trấn 127 km, the city Hoàng Vân 150 km. Map crop: a small river between a bare grey mountain ridge with a lake and the sea beyond to the west and rolling golden grassland to the east; oak woods fill the foot of the mountains; a lake lies to the south.
places.imagined: A golden autumn morning: the great ginkgo has turned in one night, and the roofs are carpeted yellow.
places.subject: The place: Ngân Hạnh Thôn, Ginkgo Village, seen from above in autumn. Setting: oak woods in russet and green at the foot of a bare grey mountain ridge, rolling golden grassland spreading east, a lake and the sea glimpsed to the west, a small clear river winding through, and a few fields. In a clearing beside the river stands one colossal ginkgo tree, about sixty metres tall, its crown ninety metres across, which dwarfs the village; it has turned completely golden-yellow, a vast globe of gold, with a carpet of fallen yellow leaves spreading in a wide circle under it. The village is about forty grey-tile houses gathered under and around its crown, with yellow leaves covering the roofs and yards, small lanes, a round stone terrace around the trunk with benches, a roadside stall roasting nuts over charcoal with a column of smoke, and a small wooden bridge. The fields beyond are small, hedged plots. Villagers sweep leaves in groups, children throw them, and a few people sit on the stone terrace looking up. The oak woods behind are dull gold against the tree's brilliant yellow. Low soft golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The ginkgo's trunk takes eleven people with arms outstretched to encircle, and its lowest branch carries a swing. Stone steps, a roadside shrine and a long communal table stand beneath it. Fallen leaves are swept every dawn into heaps as tall as a man, and the carts of nut-roasters stand in a row along the river road, each with a charcoal brazier. The houses are low, built of grey brick and timber, their lanes radiating from the tree like spokes.

places.name: Lý Hoa Thôn
places.size: A fishing hamlet of about 30 houses and 120 people, with an orchard of about 400 white plum trees down to the high-tide line.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on a sandy beach, coast. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the spirit vein Bạch Nhạn Huyệt 180 km. Map crop: the southern shore of a round blue bay, with a forested shore across it to the north and low grassy hills behind; a small stream runs to the sea at the village.
places.imagined: Early spring: the orchard so white that beach and blossom are hard to tell apart, snow geese among the branches.
places.subject: The place: Lý Hoa Thôn, Plum Blossom Village, seen from above a sandy beach in early spring. Setting: a long pale sand beach curving along the southern shore of a round bay of calm grey-blue sea, low surf, a few rocks, a dark forested shore across the bay to the north, and low grass hills behind. Behind the beach, a plum orchard of about four hundred trees in neat rows runs right down to the high-tide line, every tree in full white bloom, so the orchard is a snowfield of white that is almost indistinguishable from the pale sand, the two blending at the edge. Dozens of grey snow geese sit among the branches and walk on the sand among fallen petals. Behind the orchard stand about thirty small houses of grey stone with thatch roofs, with fish drying on racks, nets hung on poles, a smoke house, and a small shrine. A dozen fishing boats with brown sails are drawn up in a line on the sand below, with tiny figures mending nets and launching a boat. A footpath of white-grey shell leads through the trees. Cold clear light from the upper left, long faint shadows to the lower right. The orchard is arranged in thirty rows of thirteen trees, with a track of crushed shell between each pair, and the lowest row stands in drifted sand at the high-tide line. Ground cover of white petals gives the sand beneath a faint pinkish tint. A salt-drying yard of shallow pans lies beside the boat slips. Four geese walk the sand beside a fisherwoman mending a net, while a boy chases them with a stick. Smoke from drying racks drifts through the blossom.

places.name: Hoàng Ngưu Thôn
places.size: A cattle village of about 45 houses and 200 people beside a round corral about 120 m across, with herds of several hundred yellow oxen.
places.where: Open grassland at 20 m, inland. Wood qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Nearest: the lake Triêu Hà Hồ 90 km, the lake Minh Kính Hồ 90 km. Named from the wild oxen on the plain left empty after Cửu Thiều fell. Map crop: a gold-green plain on the east side of a long blue lake, with a bare grey ridge beyond the lake and the sea to the west; several darker forest bands cross the plain.
places.imagined: First day of spring: one ox with red-painted horns being walked round the corral.
places.subject: The place: Hoàng Ngưu Thôn, Yellow Ox Village, seen from above an open plain. Setting: wide green and golden grassland reaching east, a long blue lake lying along the west side with a bare grey ridge beyond it, and a few low trees. Beside a great round corral about a hundred and twenty metres across, made of piled fieldstone in a thick ring wall, sit about forty-five grey-tile houses in a loose crescent with yards, ox sheds, hay barns with stacks, a trough and a well. In and around the corral are hundreds of yellow oxen: herds of them grazing loosely all around across the plain, tawny and broad-shouldered, and the grass near the corral is worn to bare earth in a wide pale ring. Tracks of hooves radiate along the plain. Inside the corral a ring of herders walks round one ox whose horns are painted red, with villagers gathered along the wall, a tiny crowd. Ox-drawn ploughs and carts with great wheels stand ready, a cart road runs off toward the rice plain. Golden light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right, a light haze of dust from the herds. The corral wall is thirty courses of fieldstone high, with a heavy wooden gate on rollers, and a raised walkway runs around its top for the herders. Water troughs of hollowed logs stand along the inside. The oxen's yokes hang in rows under an open cart shed, and a farrier works at an anvil in the lee of the wall. Tracks of hooves, pale on the worn ground, fan out in a hundred lanes. A drover on a spotted horse leads a herd of fifty along the lake road.

places.name: Triêu Hà Hồ
places.size: A great lake of grassland country: on the map about 80 km wide and running off the frame north and south; a stone platform about 80 m across half awash in the eastern shallows, and a small sect shrine (the Dawn Hall) of about 20 buildings on its shore.
places.where: A lake at -40 m in open grassland, inland. Wood qi. No holder; beside Lễ Tuyền Phái, whose seat moved to its shore (the Dawn Hall) in 1141. Nearest: the town Lục Dã 90 km, the village Hoàng Ngưu 90 km. Dawn clouds answer Lạc Hà's sunset clouds in the west. Map crop: a huge long blue lake, about 80 km wide, running off the frame to the north and south between golden-green grassland on the east and a ridge of bare grey crags on the west with the sea beyond; a river joins its south end.
places.imagined: Dawn. The lake so still that the clouds lie doubled on it, rose mist turning gold.
places.subject: The place: Triêu Hà Hồ, the Dawn Cloud Lake, seen from high above at sunrise. Setting: a vast shallow lake some eighty kilometres across that runs off the frame to the north and south, between golden-green grassland on the east and a ridge of bare grey crags on the west with the sea beyond it, its surface so still that the first clouds of dawn lie doubled upon it, a mirror of pink, rose and gold; a mist rises off the water in slow curls and turns rose, then gold, with the sunrise. Reed beds and shallow sandbars fringe the shore in pale green, and the grassland beyond is dark blue-green in the last shadow. In the eastern shallows lies a low flat platform of weathered stone about eighty metres across, half awash, ringed by broken stumps of pillars where musicians once played to the sun, with the water lapping across it in a thin sheet. On the western shore stands the Dawn Hall of a small sect, a modest walled compound of about twenty pale timber buildings with a three-roofed pagoda, a landing stage and a few boats, with a small spring basin. A flock of white cranes stands in the shallows, and a few boats with tiny figures drift out to meet the sun. Low sunlight from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. Fishing boats with square sails dot the far water, tiny against the lake's scale. The Dawn Hall's wall is whitewashed, and eight of its buildings are two-storeyed brewing halls with open eaves for the sweet-spring wine. The stone platform's edge is a ring of twelve stub pillars, and fine ripples run across its flagged floor. Where the reeds thicken, hundreds of cranes stand in pairs on one leg, and mist wraps the lake's whole length in a rose-gold band.

places.name: Vân Môn Thành
places.size: A ruined city: walls about 2 km on a side, once some 12,000 roofs, now a grass-grown square with stumps of towers; one upright stone frame at its centre.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on a river, inland. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. A former city of Cửu Thiều Cung, built 130, abandoned after the War of the Nine Shao. Nearest: the spirit vein Cửu Tấu Mạch 103 km, Lễ Tuyền Phái 127 km. Map crop: a river running down a golden-green hill plain toward a blue bay at the lower right, with bare grey crags on the left edge and dry hills all around.
places.imagined: Strong wind, the empty stone frame humming a low note.
places.subject: The place: Vân Môn Thành, the ruined City of the Cloud Gate, seen from above. Setting: a grassland river plain, pale in a dry windy season, a slow river running down the plain to a blue bay at the lower right, bare grey crags along the left edge, wind combing the long grass in waves. What was a great city is now low grass-grown walls broken into a rough square about two kilometres on a side, with gaps where gates stood, the stumps of towers at the corners and in places along the wall, and a shallow dry moat. Inside, the street grid still shows as faint straight lines in the grass, with foundation lines of thousands of buildings as low mounds and square outlines, a few broken stone arches, a dry canal, and a collapsed bridge on the river. In the middle stands the one thing still upright: a tall frame of two carved stone pillars about twenty metres high with a crossbeam, where a stone chime once hung in the city's hall, a thin dark shape against the grass, with a long shadow. A herder's small camp, a few tents and a flock of sheep, lies sheltered in the lee of the wall far from the frame, tiny figures. A pale band of dust blows across. Light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. A pair of carved stone lion bases, each three metres wide, guard the vanished south gate, and a stone-lined well still holds clear water at the city's centre. The stone frame's cross-beam bears a row of eight empty iron rings from which the chime hung. Footings of the vanished hall show as a large rectangle of pale paving with a few column bases. Herders' stone windbreaks, waist-high, make a loose ring in the lee of the north wall, and the sheep flock moves like a dust cloud among the mounds.

places.name: Châu Lệ Cảng
places.size: A burned harbour town: about 1.5 km of curved shoreline, once some 4,000 roofs, now charred shells, piers and a heap of oyster shell beach.
places.where: Grassland at sea level on the coast. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung. Once a city; Phượng Minh's pearl harbour built in 600 and burned in 762 by Thôn Hải's pirates. Nearest: the minor seat Vọng Triều Đường 180 km. Map crop: the head of a blue bay at the foot of golden-green hills, with a river running in from the south and a small lake in the south; the ruin sits on the bay's southern shore.
places.imagined: Moonlight on the water over the old oyster beds, glowing faintly; fishers pass without stopping.
places.subject: The place: Châu Lệ Cảng, the Harbour of Pearl Tears, a burned harbour, seen from above at dusk. Setting: a curve of low coast where grass meets a beach of heaped white oyster shells, a calm bay of dark blue water, and a pale moon rising over the sea. The beach is a long curve about a kilometre and a half long, glittering white with heaped oyster shells in banks metres high. Rows of charred pier pilings, hundreds of black stumps in lines, stand in the shallows where the piers ran out to the harbour. Behind them the burned shells of warehouses, long roofless buildings with blackened stone walls, slope down into the sea; a broken harbour wall runs out and collapses into the water. Above the beach the town was a grid of about four thousand roofs, now rows of roofless house walls grown with grass and creeper, with burn marks, a broken lighthouse stump, and the open frame of a burned great hall. Over the oyster beds the water glows faintly pale green. A single fishing boat far out passes without stopping, with a tiny figure. Moonlight and the last dusk glow from the upper left, cool shadows. Burned pier pilings run in eleven rows, each about two hundred metres long, and ribbed iron brackets still cling to some. The oyster banks are heaped to the height of a house in places, white against the green-blue water, and the lighthouse stump is a squat black cylinder seven metres across. Roofless warehouse walls have trees growing in them, and a few climbing roses run wild over the burned governor's hall. Where the old quay stood a low line of blackened stone points seaward, and a single fisher's boat is moored beyond the surf, its crew looking away.

places.name: Vọng Triều Đường
places.size: A minor sect of lamp-keepers: about 50 sworn keepers, twelve lamp towers (nine lit) along about 2 km of coast, about 35 buildings.
places.where: Steppe at 50 m on the coast, 7 tiles from the burned piers of Châu Lệ Cảng. Water qi. A vassal of Phượng Minh Cung, righteous, founded 790. Nearest: the ruin Châu Lệ Cảng 180 km. Map crop: steppe of green-gold grass on the western shore of a great blue bay, with a river winding down from the west, one dark stand of trees inland, and a rocky shore of pale shingle.
places.imagined: Night. Nine of twelve lamp towers lit along a steppe coast, three dark.
places.subject: The place: Vọng Triều Đường, the Hall of Watching the Tide, a small sect of lamp keepers, seen from above a steppe coast at dusk. Setting: a low steppe of green-gold grass above the western shore of a great blue bay, with slow surf, a long shore of pale shingle, a few rock stacks, a small river winding down from the west, one dark stand of pines inland, and a dark sky with the first stars. The compound is a modest walled yard of about thirty-five buildings of whitewashed stone with grey slate roofs: a main hall, long dormitories, a kitchen, a store of lamp oil in a row of round tanks, and a small tide-pool garden. Along about two kilometres of the shore, spaced roughly evenly, stand twelve lamp towers, tapering white stone towers about thirty metres tall with a glass-walled lamp room at the top: nine of them are lit, throwing long pale beams out over the water and sending a golden glow down the coast, three are dark with their lamps unlit. A signal flag mast and a causeway run to the nearest tower. Keepers in white robes are tiny figures on the galleries and on the paths between towers, a few carrying oil jars. Dusk light from the upper left, with warm lamp glow. The lamp towers are numbered in stone over each door, and twelve long oil stairs, each of two hundred steps, are worn in the middle. Three of the unlit towers have scaffolding of lashed timber at their foot, where keepers are rebuilding the lamp rooms. The oil tanks are painted black, ten of them, and a mule-driven pump lifts oil to the towers through lead pipes. Beacon-fire signals are laid ready in iron baskets at each gallery, and the keepers' vows are cut in a row of small stones along the causeway.
